chunks.heading: What does n! mean?
chunks.body: n! (n factorial) means multiplying every whole number from n down to 1. For example, 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24.
chunks.checkText: What is 3!?

chunks.heading: Why is 0! equal to 1?
chunks.body: By definition, 0! is set to equal 1, not 0. This makes formulas built from [[mathext1-factorial-notation|factorials]] work correctly even when nothing is left to arrange.
chunks.checkText: What does 0! equal?

chunks.heading: The multiplication principle
chunks.body: If a choice is made in several stages, multiply the number of options at each stage together to find the total number of outcomes.
chunks.checkText: You have 3 shirts and 4 hats. Using the multiplication principle, how many outfits can you make?

chunks.heading: Counting with repeats allowed
chunks.body: When choosing r items in order from n options, and repeats are allowed, the [[mathext1-multiplication-principle|multiplication principle]] gives n^r total ways, since each choice has n options.
chunks.checkText: How many 3-digit codes can you make from the digits 0-9, if digits can repeat?

chunks.heading: What is a permutation?
chunks.body: A permutation is an arrangement of items in a particular order, where no item is repeated. Swapping the order of two items always creates a different permutation.
chunks.checkText: In a permutation, does the order of the items matter?

chunks.heading: Counting permutations without repeats
chunks.body: The number of ways to arrange r items chosen in order from n distinct items, with no repeats, is written nPr and equals n!/(n − r)!.
chunks.checkText: Which formula gives the number of ordered arrangements of r items chosen from n, without repetition?

chunks.heading: Arranging every item in a set
chunks.body: When you arrange all n items in a set (r = n), the [[mathext1-permutations-formula|permutations formula]] simplifies to nPn = n!, since (n − n)! = 0! = 1.
chunks.checkText: In how many ways can 5 different books be lined up on a shelf?

chunks.heading: Deal with restrictions first
chunks.body: When a counting problem has a rule about where certain items must go, place those restricted items into position before counting the ways to arrange everything else.
chunks.checkText: When a counting problem has a special restriction, the best first step is usually to...

chunks.heading: Keeping some items together
chunks.body: To arrange items where a few must stay together, treat that group as a single block first, order the blocks, then order the items inside the block separately.
chunks.checkText: To count arrangements where two people must sit together, it helps to first treat them as...

chunks.heading: Counting what you don't want
chunks.body: Sometimes it's easier to count every possible arrangement, then subtract the ones that break a rule, rather than counting the allowed arrangements directly.
chunks.checkText: If a problem asks for arrangements where two people are NOT next to each other, a good approach is to...

checkOptions.text: Subtract the 'together' arrangements from the total
Only count the times they are together

chunks.heading: Splitting a problem into cases
chunks.body: When one counting method can't cover every possibility at once, split the problem into separate, non-overlapping cases, count each one, then add the results together.
chunks.checkText: When using cases to solve a counting problem, the cases should be...

chunks.heading: Arranging letters that repeat
chunks.body: If a word has repeated letters, divide n! by the [[mathext1-factorial-notation|factorial]] of each repeat count, since swapping identical letters doesn't create a new arrangement.
chunks.checkText: The word 'BOB' has 3 letters, with the letter B repeated twice. How many distinct arrangements does it have?

chunks.heading: Arranging people in a circle
chunks.body: In a circle, every seat looks the same until someone sits down, so fix one person's seat first. The rest can then be arranged in (n − 1)! ways.
chunks.checkText: In how many ways can 6 people be seated around a circular table?

chunks.heading: Grouping around a circle
chunks.body: To seat groups around a circle, first order the items inside each group, then use the same idea as [[mathext1-circular-arrangements|circular arrangements]] to place the groups themselves.
chunks.checkText: To seat 3 couples around a circular table so each couple sits together, you should first...

checkOptions.text: Order each couple, then arrange the 3 couples in a circle
Ignore the couples and seat everyone randomly
Only count the seating of one couple

chunks.heading: Order matters, or it doesn't
chunks.body: Picking a class captain and vice-captain from 3 friends cares about order (2 different roles). Picking any 2 friends for a group project doesn't — that's a combination, not a [[mathext1-permutation-definition|permutation]].
chunks.checkText: Choosing 2 winners for two identical prizes from a group of friends is an example of a...

chunks.heading: How many subsets does a set have?
chunks.body: A set with n members has 2^n possible subsets in total, including the empty subset. Each item is either included or left out, giving 2 choices per item.
chunks.checkText: How many subsets does a 4-member set have in total?

chunks.heading: Counting combinations: nCr
chunks.body: The number of ways to choose r items from n, where order doesn't matter, is written nCr and equals n!/(r! × (n − r)!).
chunks.checkText: Which formula counts the number of unordered selections of r items from n?

chunks.heading: Choosing who's in, or who's out
chunks.body: Choosing r items to include from n is the same as choosing the other (n − r) items to leave out. That's why [[mathext1-combination-formula|nCr]] always equals nC(n − r).
chunks.checkText: For a group of 10 people, which pair of values must be equal?

chunks.heading: Using counting to find probability
chunks.body: To find a probability, count the favourable outcomes and divide by the total number of outcomes, using [[mathext1-combination-formula|nCr]] or [[mathext1-permutations-formula|nPr]] to count each one.

chunks.heading: The pigeonhole principle
chunks.body: If more items are placed into a smaller number of groups, at least one group must contain more than one item. For example, 11 pigeons in 10 holes means some hole has at least 2.
chunks.checkText: If 13 people are in a room, why must at least two of them share a birth month?

checkOptions.text: 13 people but only 12 months, so the pigeonhole principle guarantees a shared month
Birth months are always evenly spread

chunks.heading: A stronger pigeonhole rule
chunks.body: If n items are placed into d groups, at least one group must hold at least the average, rounded up. With 31 pigeons in 10 holes, some hole has at least 4, since 31 ÷ 10 rounds up to 4.
chunks.checkText: If 25 lollies are shared among 4 kids, why must at least one kid get at least 7?

checkOptions.text: 25 ÷ 4 = 6 remainder 1, so one kid must have more than 6
Every kid always gets exactly the same amount
It only applies to actual pigeons

chunks.heading: What is a binomial?
chunks.body: A binomial is an expression with exactly two terms added or subtracted, like x + y or 1 − 3x. Raising one to a power, like (x + y)^n, is a binomial expansion.
chunks.checkText: Which of these is a binomial?

chunks.heading: Expanding powers of a binomial
chunks.body: Expanding [[mathext1-binomial-definition|(1 + x)^n]] for increasing values of n produces coefficients that build up a triangular pattern, known as Pascal's triangle.
chunks.checkText: The coefficients you get from expanding (1 + x)^n for different values of n form a pattern called...

chunks.heading: Every row starts and ends with 1
chunks.body: In [[mathext1-binomial-expansion-intro|Pascal's triangle]], the first and last number in every row is always 1, no matter how far down the triangle you go.
chunks.checkText: What are the first and last numbers in every row of Pascal's triangle?

chunks.heading: Pascal's triangle is symmetric
chunks.body: Each row of [[mathext1-binomial-expansion-intro|Pascal's triangle]] reads the same forwards and backwards. For example, the row 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 is a mirror image of itself.
chunks.checkText: Row 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1 of Pascal's triangle is an example of a row that is...

chunks.heading: Building each row from the row above
chunks.body: Apart from the 1s, every number in Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two numbers directly above it in the row before.
chunks.checkText: In Pascal's triangle, a number (other than a 1) is found by...

checkOptions.text: Adding the two numbers above it
Multiplying the row number by itself

chunks.heading: How many terms in an expansion?
chunks.body: Expanding [[mathext1-binomial-definition|(x + y)^n]] always produces n + 1 terms in total, one more than the power n itself.
chunks.checkText: How many terms are in the expansion of (x + y)^5?

chunks.heading: Expanding (x + y)^n
chunks.body: In each term of [[mathext1-binomial-definition|(x + y)^n]], the powers of x and y always add up to n. The coefficients still come from [[mathext1-binomial-expansion-intro|Pascal's triangle]].
chunks.checkText: In the expansion of (x + y)^6, the powers of x and y in every single term add up to...

chunks.heading: The binomial theorem
chunks.body: The binomial theorem says the coefficient of x^(n−r) y^r in the expansion of [[mathext1-binomial-expansion-xy|(x + y)^n]] is exactly [[mathext1-combination-formula|nCr]]. This links counting to algebra.
chunks.checkText: According to the binomial theorem, the coefficient of the term containing y^r in (x + y)^n is...

chunks.heading: Three values worth memorising
chunks.body: For any whole number n: nC0 = 1, nC1 = n, and nC2 = n(n − 1)/2. These come straight from the start of every row in [[mathext1-binomial-expansion-intro|Pascal's triangle]].
chunks.checkText: What does nC1 always equal?

chunks.heading: Adding up a whole row
chunks.body: The numbers in row n of [[mathext1-binomial-expansion-intro|Pascal's triangle]] always add up to 2^n, matching the [[mathext1-subset-counting-power-of-two|total number of subsets]] of an n-member set.
chunks.checkText: What do all the numbers in row 5 of Pascal's triangle add up to?

chunks.heading: Finding one term without expanding everything
chunks.body: Using the [[mathext1-binomial-theorem|binomial theorem]], you can jump straight to one specific term of an expansion — like the term in x^3 — without writing out every term first.
chunks.checkText: To find just the x^3 term in a large binomial expansion, the fastest method is to...

checkOptions.text: Use the binomial theorem to pick out that one term
Always expand every single term first
